title: Experimental reproduction numbers disentangle vaccine effects on susceptibility and infectiousness during H5N1 transmission in geese
abstract: Vaccination against high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) is increasingly used to protect poultry, but vaccine performance is commonly inferred from clinical protection and virus shedding rather than measured transmission. We asked whether reproduction numbers from controlled transmission experiments can quantify how vaccination changes susceptibility and infectiousness. Domestic geese were prime-boost vaccinated with an H5 clade 2.3.4.4b RNA-replicon vaccine and challenged with homologous HPAIV H5N1. Replicated seeder-sentinel groups represented transmission among unvaccinated animals, to vaccinated contacts, and from vaccinated breakthrough-infected animals. Vaccinated directly challenged geese remained clinically protected although all became RT-qPCR-positive. Estimated reproduction numbers were R0=4.7 (95% CI, 2.8-8.0) among unvaccinated geese, Rs=2.6 (1.6-4.5) for transmission to vaccinated contacts, Ri=3.7 (2.0-6.8) for transmission from vaccinated infected geese, and Rvacc=2.0 (0.8-4.9) for a fully vaccinated population. Vaccination reduced transmission but did not reduce the point estimate for Rvacc below one under these intensive exposure conditions. Vaccinated infected geese also shed substantially less viral RNA, whereas the estimated reduction in infectiousness was more modest, indicating that RNA shedding alone may not reliably predict transmission reduction. Experimental reproduction numbers therefore provide a direct population-level complement to conventional vaccine endpoints and separate effects on susceptibility from effects on onward transmission.

title: Climate Factors, Air Pollutants, and Extreme Events Shape Influenza Risk in China: A Hospital-Based Case-Crossover and Machine-Learning Study
abstract: Abstract Although the link between seasonal influenza and environment has been established, the heterogeneous impacts of climate extreme events with their interactions remain poorly understood. Based on 630,120 influenza-positive cases from hospitals in 335 Chinese cities (2005–2019), this case-crossover study adopted distributed lag nonlinear models to quantify exposure-lag-response relationships between environmental exposures and influenza, applied machine learning to rank dominant variables, and performed a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model using Beijing as proof of concept to test the forecasting utility of extreme events. Meteorological variables, air pollution, and extreme events are significantly associated with influenza risk. abstract_zh: 摘要 尽管季节性流感与环境之间的联系已被确立,但气候极端事件及其相互作用的异质性影响仍了解甚少。本病例交叉研究基于2005年至2019年间中国335个城市的630,120例流感阳性病例,采用分布式滞后非线性模型量化环境暴露与流感之间的暴露-滞后-反应关系,应用机器学习对主导变量进行排序,并在北京采用长短期记忆(LSTM)模型作为概念验证,以测试极端事件的预测效用。气象变量、空气污染和极端事件均与流感风险显著相关。机器学习模型表明,大气温度、湿度和颗粒物可能是主要贡献因素。同时暴露于极端事件显示出比单一暴露更高的联合风险,其在乘法尺度上表现出显著的次乘法相互作用,未发现加法相互作用的证据。基于北京特定的LSTM概念验证框架,将极端事件整合到模型中显著提升了每日流感预测的性能。气候因素、空气污染和极端事件可能塑造流感风险,其在亚型、人口统计学特征和地理区域之间表现出异质性影响。这些发现强调了在气候变化时代将极端气候事件整合到流感预测和精准公共卫生响应中的潜在益处。

title: Air sampling in team congregate spaces for early detection of respiratory virus threats at the 2026 FIFA World CupTM
abstract: Respiratory infections are the leading cause of illness at major sporting events, yet surveillance relies on athletes recognising and reporting symptoms, missing asymptomatic, pre-symptomatic and unreported infections. During competitions, teams are housed together and share spaces with members of the broader community. To evaluate whether continuous air sampling with point-of-care testing could detect respiratory-virus nucleic acids in an elite team's congregate spaces during competition, and whether the signals were operationally useful. Prospective, descriptive environmental-surveillance study following the Canadian men's national soccer team across five host cities during the 2026 FIFA World Cup (3 June to 4 July 2026). InBio Apollo bioaerosol samplers ran continuously in up to four team-designated rooms per hotel (physiotherapy, meal, equipment and coaches' room or hallway); filters were changed approximately twice daily, eluted on-site and tested with the Cepheid Xpert(R) Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus assay. A sample was considered positive if any cycle-threshold (Ct) value was reported, as less than 45, for a target. Of 174 air filters, 13 yielded detections of viral genetic material (9 SARS-CoV-2, 3 influenza A virus, 1 influenza B virus, 0 RSV). Detections were sparse early and clustered late in the tournament. An influenza A signal appeared the morning a player was sent home febrile, and SARS-CoV-2 signals coincided with visibly ill hotel staff, with signals falling after ill staff were excluded. Air sampling with point-of-care testing is feasible in the context of an elite team and can surface behavior-independent viral signals during competition that may offer opportunities for earlier precautionary actions.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of continuous air sampling with point-of-care testing for detecting respiratory viruses in elite team congregate spaces during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The Canadian men's national soccer team was followed across five host cities, with air samplers deployed in designated rooms. Of 174 air filters, 13 tested positive for viral genetic material, including 9 SARS-CoV-2, 3 influenza A virus, and 1 influenza B virus. Detections were sparse early in the tournament and clustered later, coinciding with instances of illness among hotel staff and players. The findings suggest that air sampling could identify viral signals independently of human behavior, offering potential for earlier intervention. However, the study does not report limitations or evidence strength assessment.

full_text: Article summary AI generated Seasonal influenza poses significant health risks globally, making vaccination a crucial preventive measure. This study demonstrated that a structured educational intervention significantly improved university students' knowledge and attitudes towards the seasonal influenza vaccine in Iraq, leading to increased vaccination uptake. Abstract Background & aim Influenza is a serious viral respiratory disease, and vaccination is the primary means of prevention. The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention program in improving university students’ knowledge and attitudes regarding the seasonal influenza vaccine. Materials and methods A quasi-experimental design was employed, with convenience sampling of 204 students (102 intervention, 102 control) over a period of six months at Thi-Qar University (TQU) in southern Iraq, across six colleges selected via a simple random lottery. Students’ knowledge and attitudes were measured using a structured educational program, brochures, and pre- and post-tests. Independent- and paired-samples t-tests were used to analyze the data, with a significance level of p < 0.05. Results At pre-test, 40.2% of the intervention group had low knowledge (M ± SD = 1.68 ± 0.616); at post-test, 55.9% had high knowledge (M ± SD = 1.73 ± 0.448). In terms of attitudes, 73.5% of participants reported positive attitudes after the intervention, while 26.5% reported negative attitudes, a decrease from pre-test, where 60.8% stated that they had negative attitudes. Conclusion Significant change in knowledge and attitudes in relation to seasonal influenza vaccine following intervention (p < 0.001). A structured educational intervention is an effective strategy to increase university students’ acceptance of flu vaccines in Iraq. University-based influenza vaccination programs are recommended to improve vaccine coverage and reduce influenza-related disease. 1 Introduction Globally, influenza is a severe viral respiratory illness that significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Human illness could be caused by influenza virus types A, B, and C. Because of its high vulnerability to antigenic change, influenza A is the type most frequently responsible for pandemics [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that one billion people worldwide are affected by seasonal influenza each year, which causes between 290,000 and 650,000 influenza-associated respiratory deaths and 3–5 million episodes of severe illness [2]. Even though there are several antiviral medications that have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and are accessible in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR), vaccination is still thought to be the most effective way to prevent influenza. These vaccinations only provide protection against the vaccine antigen, and their effectiveness diminishes with time [3, 4]. Yearly, the Centers for Disease Prevention and Control (CDC) recommends individuals that aged from six months of age and older to get the seasonal influenza vaccine. The most common kind of vaccine is an intramuscular inactivated vaccine that contains a killed virus strain [5, 6]. Influenza vaccines can prevent morbidity and mortality andlessen the spread and severity of the disease. They are safe and generally well tolerated, do not cause influenza disease, and very rarely have major adverse effects. They are also essential in lowering the health and economic burden of influenza [7, 8]. Influenza outbreaks typically happen in the final autumn and all winter months. Adults should receive a yearly injection of a single dose (0.5 cc) of an influenza vaccination, ideally by October. For best results, children ages 6 months to 8 years need to receive two doses of the influenza vaccine during their first immunization season, spaced at least 4 weeks apart [9, 10]. Globally, several intervention and survey studies have explored educational strategies to increase influenza vaccination knowledge and attitudes. Abushouk et al. 2023 reported that the targeted educational interventions had a significant effect on the knowledge and practice of health sciences university students regarding the seasonal influenza vaccine in Saudi Arabia [11]. Similarly, Walker et al. (2016) conducted a study amongst medical students in Australia, which found that knowledge and attitudes were strongly linked to vaccination uptake, highlighting the importance of structured learning in improving vaccine uptake [12]. The results of this study suggest that educational programs can be effective in addressing knowledge gaps and vaccine hesitancy across a variety of cultural contexts, supporting the rationale for the current study. To assess the effectiveness of intervention program regarding seasonal influenza vaccine among university students and to enhance vaccination coverage the present study was conducted. 2 Methods Study design: quasi- experimental design was selected to obtain the current study aims. Study period: the study period was 6 months starting from 1st September to the end of February. Data collection was done by working two days per week. The applying of intervention program was continued for 4 months. Study setting: the study was conducted at Thi-qar university, Al- Nasiryiah city, southern Iraq at 6 college out of 18 colleges at the university. The colleges were selected randomly. Study Population: The students of selected colleges of the University were recruited. 17 students from each college were chosen based on a proportional allocation to achieve a total sample of approximately 102 participants per group (17 × 6 = 102), which was determined to be sufficient based on a power analysis (power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, medium effect size) to detect significant differences in knowledge and attitude scores. 2.1 An intervention group definition The intervention health education program involved four months of structured education through face-to-face lectures (on influenza etiology, transmission, complications and vaccine safety/efficacy); distribution of informational brochures, and interactive question and answer sessions. The intervention group consisted of university students who participated in this education program about seasonal influenza vaccine. 2.2 A control group definition The control group included 102 students (17 students from each of the same 6 colleges) matched to the intervention group by college and academic year that were not went received intervention program on seasonal influenza vaccine. Study Hypothesis: The current study hypothesis display that if there is a significant or non-significant relationship between study variables. - H0: suggest no significant association between pre and post intervention of student knowledge & attitudes regarding seasonal influenza vaccine. - H1: suggest significant association between pre and post intervention of student knowledge & attitudes regarding seasonal influenza vaccine. Study Sample: Convenience sample consisting from 204 students (102 study& 102 control) who eligible to participate and fitted the inclusion criteria. The inclusion criteria were student from different colleges and different stages, while the exclusion criteria were student who don’t complete the intervention program lectures in addition to those who got a score more than 80% at pretest. Study Tools: Pre-test was conducted on student’s introduction of constructed educational programs, brochures and questionnaire to assess students’ knowledge and attitude about seasonal influenza vaccine, then post test was conducted after implementation of intervention program to determine the impact of intervention program. The questionnaire consisted of three parts: (1) Demographic information sheet, and age, gender, residence, and academic specialization; (2) Knowledge sheet, comprising 15 items which assessed students’ knowledge about influenza disease, its complications, influenza transmission routes, and the influenza vaccine (types of vaccine, safety, efficacy, and influenza vaccine schedule); and (3) Attitude sheet, comprising 10 items which assessed students’ attitudes toward influenza vaccine, perceived necessity, and perceived safety perceptions of the influenza vaccine. Ranging and Scoring: A three-point Likert scale was used for rating all knowledge items (Yes = 2, Uncertain = 1, No = 0) and attitude items (Agree = 2, Neutral = 1, Disagree = 0) [13]. The questionnaire was adapted from validated questionnaires that were used in previous studies [14, 15] and administered in Arabic, the students’ native language. The instrument was first tested on a sample of 20 students (not in the final sample) for clarity, comprehension and timing, and slight changes were made to the instrument based on this pilot testing. A panel of five expert nurses and public health experts confirmed the content validity. The degree of knowledge and attitudes were assessed by the cutoff point and by the mean score. The mean score for each part was computed by adding up all item scores and dividing into three parts: (i) Low (< 33rd percentile), (ii) Fair (33rd–66th percentile) and (iii) High (> 66th percentile) for knowledge; and Negative (< mean) and Positive (≥ mean) for attitudes. The mean was calculated using neutral/uncertain responses given as intermediate (score = 1). Statistical analysis: SPSS version 26 was used to analyze data. The present study used descriptive and inferential statistics such as mean, standard deviation (SD), independent samples t-test and paired samples t-test. A level of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 Results Table 1 shows the descriptive results of the present study. In terms of gender, 58.8% of the intervention group were females and 41.2% were males, whereas 54.9% of the control group were female and 45.1% were male. As for age, 49.0% of those in the intervention group were in the age group of 18 to 20 years while 52.9% of those in the control group were in the age group of 21 to 25 years. In regard to place of residence, the proportion of each group who lived in urban areas (53.9% and 66.7%, respectively) was higher for both intervention and control groups. Lastly, of the student specializations, 69.6% of the intervention group and 51.0% of the control group were scientific. In the intervention group, results displayed that (40.2%) of students have a low knowledge regarding seasonal influenza vaccine at period of the pre-test with M ± SD (1.68±0.616). While at period of the post-test, findings showed that (55.9%) declared a high knowledge level with M ± SD equal to (1.73±0.448). The control group expressed 49.0% of student have a fair knowledge regarding seasonal influenza vaccine at pre and post test period with M ± SD (2.04±0.716), Table 2, 3 revealed that 60.8% of students at intervention group and 67.6% of student at control group have a negative attitude regarding seasonal influenza vaccine at pre- test period where the M ± SD was (1.39±0.491, 1.32±0.470) respectively. While at post- test period the study group demonstrated 73.5% of students have a positive attitude regarding seasonal influenza vaccine and 67.6% of students at control group have a negative attitude. The current results showed at Table 4, there was a highly statistically difference in overall assessment of student knowledge, vaccination status, family vaccination history and attitudes between two periods pre and post applying the intervention program among university students where the p- value for all variables was (< 0.001). Table 5 demonstrated that no statistical difference in students’ knowledge regarding seasonal influenza vaccine was found between intervention and control group at pre- test period (t=-1.599; p = 0.111, 95% CI: -0.328 to 0.034) while there was a highly statistical difference in students’ knowledge at post test period between two groups where (t = 6.194; p < 0.001, 95% CI: 0.408 to 0.788). In respect to students’ vaccination status at pre -test periods, no statistical association was found between intervention and control groups (t = 1.497; p = 0.136, 95% CI: -0.031 to 0.227) but at post - intervention program there was a statistically association found between both groups (t= -7.361; p = 0.000). According to students’ family vaccination status the present outcome reveal that no difference was found at pre- intervention between study and control group (t= -1.616; p = 0.108, 95% CI: -0.348 to 0.035), in contrast to the post intervention program applying there was a statistical difference in students family vaccination status between both groups (t = 7.694; p = 0.000). Finally, regarding students attitudes, no statistical differences was found at pre- intervention between intervention and control group (t = 1.020; p = 0.309, 95% CI: -0.064 to 0.201) but in other hand there was a statistical difference between both groups at post intervention program applying period (t = 6.435; p < 0.001, 95% CI: 0.286 to 0.538). 4 Discussion The purpose of the present study was to examine if an intervention program would have a positive effect on university students’ knowledge and attitude towards seasonal influenza vaccine in Thi Qar University, Iraq. The results showed the importance of the intervention program to students’ knowledge, attitudes and vaccination status. 4.1 Knowledge regarding seasonal influenza vaccine In intervention group, before intervention, 40.2% of students had low knowledge and 7.8% had high knowledge on seasonal influenza vaccine. This finding concurs with the numerous studies that have been conducted in the Middle East region previously which have consistently indicated little knowledge on influenza vaccination among university students. After the intervention, level of knowledge improved substantially − 55.9% of students in the intervention group contrasted to 27.5% in the control group. After intervention, there is a highly significant difference (p = 0.000) between the groups in that structured educational programs are very effective in empowering students to learn about the seasonal influenza vaccines. Comparing to Abushouk et al. (2023), we report similar findings, where we determined that those educational interventions effectively increased knowledge about influenza vaccination in the university population [11]. 4.2 Attitudes towards seasonal influenza vaccine Before intervention, the attitude of both intervention (60.8%) and control (67.6%) groups towards seasonal influenza vaccine showed predominantly negative attitudes. This is consistent with the known general vaccine hesitancy seen across the Eastern Mediterranean Region [1, 17]. Misconceptions about vaccine safety, efficacy and necessity have been related to negative attitudes toward vaccines and to cultural and social factors which affect village (village, region) people’s health seeking behavior this is the approximately similar to Smith S. et al. (2016) and Abd K. et al. (2021) [18, 19]. Attitudes were remarkably changed in the intervention group post intervention − 73.5 vs. 32.4% of students in the control group had positive attitudes. This significant improvement (p < 0.001) is therefore indicative of the fact that well designed educational interventions can in fact address misconceptions and concerns surrounding the influenza vaccine. (2021) [12, 21]. This finding has implications as it means education does not only increase knowledge and attitude but also improve the vaccination uptake. (2020) and Sales et al. (2012) [22, 23]. Second, the status of vaccination may be subject to recall bias or social desirability bias, as it is self-reported. The study does not include a long term follow up to explore the sustainability of the knowledge gain and of attitude change. In addition, it adds to the diversity of the sample through the inclusion of students from different colleges and specializations. 4.5 Implications for practice The findings presented in this study are of key importance for public health practice in Iraq and similar environments. full_text_sections.full_text: Article summary AI generated Seasonal influenza poses significant health risks globally, making vaccination a crucial preventive measure. This study demonstrated that a structured educational intervention significantly improved university students' knowledge and attitudes towards the seasonal influenza vaccine in Iraq, leading to increased vaccination uptake. Abstract Background & aim Influenza is a serious viral respiratory disease, and vaccination is the primary means of prevention. The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention program in improving university students’ knowledge and attitudes regarding the seasonal influenza vaccine. Materials and methods A quasi-experimental design was employed, with convenience sampling of 204 students (102 intervention, 102 control) over a period of six months at Thi-Qar University (TQU) in southern Iraq, across six colleges selected via a simple random lottery. Students’ knowledge and attitudes were measured using a structured educational program, brochures, and pre- and post-tests. Independent- and paired-samples t-tests were used to analyze the data, with a significance level of p < 0.05. Results At pre-test, 40.2% of the intervention group had low knowledge (M ± SD = 1.68 ± 0.616); at post-test, 55.9% had high knowledge (M ± SD = 1.73 ± 0.448). In terms of attitudes, 73.5% of participants reported positive attitudes after the intervention, while 26.5% reported negative attitudes, a decrease from pre-test, where 60.8% stated that they had negative attitudes. Conclusion Significant change in knowledge and attitudes in relation to seasonal influenza vaccine following intervention (p < 0.001). A structured educational intervention is an effective strategy to increase university students’ acceptance of flu vaccines in Iraq. University-based influenza vaccination programs are recommended to improve vaccine coverage and reduce influenza-related disease. 1 Introduction Globally, influenza is a severe viral respiratory illness that significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Human illness could be caused by influenza virus types A, B, and C. Because of its high vulnerability to antigenic change, influenza A is the type most frequently responsible for pandemics [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that one billion people worldwide are affected by seasonal influenza each year, which causes between 290,000 and 650,000 influenza-associated respiratory deaths and 3–5 million episodes of severe illness [2]. Even though there are several antiviral medications that have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and are accessible in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR), vaccination is still thought to be the most effective way to prevent influenza. These vaccinations only provide protection against the vaccine antigen, and their effectiveness diminishes with time [3, 4]. Yearly, the Centers for Disease Prevention and Control (CDC) recommends individuals that aged from six months of age and older to get the seasonal influenza vaccine. The most common kind of vaccine is an intramuscular inactivated vaccine that contains a killed virus strain [5, 6]. Influenza vaccines can prevent morbidity and mortality andlessen the spread and severity of the disease. They are safe and generally well tolerated, do not cause influenza disease, and very rarely have major adverse effects. They are also essential in lowering the health and economic burden of influenza [7, 8]. Influenza outbreaks typically happen in the final autumn and all winter months. Adults should receive a yearly injection of a single dose (0.5 cc) of an influenza vaccination, ideally by October. For best results, children ages 6 months to 8 years need to receive two doses of the influenza vaccine during their first immunization season, spaced at least 4 weeks apart [9, 10]. Globally, several intervention and survey studies have explored educational strategies to increase influenza vaccination knowledge and attitudes. Abushouk et al. 2023 reported that the targeted educational interventions had a significant effect on the knowledge and practice of health sciences university students regarding the seasonal influenza vaccine in Saudi Arabia [11]. Similarly, Walker et al. (2016) conducted a study amongst medical students in Australia, which found that knowledge and attitudes were strongly linked to vaccination uptake, highlighting the importance of structured learning in improving vaccine uptake [12]. The results of this study suggest that educational programs can be effective in addressing knowledge gaps and vaccine hesitancy across a variety of cultural contexts, supporting the rationale for the current study. To assess the effectiveness of intervention program regarding seasonal influenza vaccine among university students and to enhance vaccination coverage the present study was conducted. 2 Methods Study design: quasi- experimental design was selected to obtain the current study aims. Study period: the study period was 6 months starting from 1st September to the end of February. Data collection was done by working two days per week. The applying of intervention program was continued for 4 months. Study setting: the study was conducted at Thi-qar university, Al- Nasiryiah city, southern Iraq at 6 college out of 18 colleges at the university. The colleges were selected randomly. Study Population: The students of selected colleges of the University were recruited. 17 students from each college were chosen based on a proportional allocation to achieve a total sample of approximately 102 participants per group (17 × 6 = 102), which was determined to be sufficient based on a power analysis (power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, medium effect size) to detect significant differences in knowledge and attitude scores. 2.1 An intervention group definition The intervention health education program involved four months of structured education through face-to-face lectures (on influenza etiology, transmission, complications and vaccine safety/efficacy); distribution of informational brochures, and interactive question and answer sessions. The intervention group consisted of university students who participated in this education program about seasonal influenza vaccine. 2.2 A control group definition The control group included 102 students (17 students from each of the same 6 colleges) matched to the intervention group by college and academic year that were not went received intervention program on seasonal influenza vaccine. Study Hypothesis: The current study hypothesis display that if there is a significant or non-significant relationship between study variables. - H0: suggest no significant association between pre and post intervention of student knowledge & attitudes regarding seasonal influenza vaccine. - H1: suggest significant association between pre and post intervention of student knowledge & attitudes regarding seasonal influenza vaccine. Study Sample: Convenience sample consisting from 204 students (102 study& 102 control) who eligible to participate and fitted the inclusion criteria. The inclusion criteria were student from different colleges and different stages, while the exclusion criteria were student who don’t complete the intervention program lectures in addition to those who got a score more than 80% at pretest. Study Tools: Pre-test was conducted on student’s introduction of constructed educational programs, brochures and questionnaire to assess students’ knowledge and attitude about seasonal influenza vaccine, then post test was conducted after implementation of intervention program to determine the impact of intervention program. The questionnaire consisted of three parts: (1) Demographic information sheet, and age, gender, residence, and academic specialization; (2) Knowledge sheet, comprising 15 items which assessed students’ knowledge about influenza disease, its complications, influenza transmis…

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the impact of an educational intervention program on university students’ knowledge and attitudes towards seasonal influenza vaccination in Iraq. Using a quasi-experimental design, 204 students were divided into intervention and control groups, with the intervention group receiving structured educational materials and brochures. Pre- and post-tests were used to measure knowledge and attitudes. Results showed a significant improvement in knowledge, with 55.9% of students achieving high knowledge levels post-intervention compared to 40.2% pre-intervention. Attitudes also shifted, with 73.5% of participants reporting positive attitudes after the intervention, down from 60.8% who had negative attitudes pre-intervention. The authors concluded that the intervention significantly improved knowledge and attitudes (p < 0.001), suggesting that structured educational programs could enhance vaccine acceptance among university students. The study’s findings have implications for public health strategies in Iraq, but the use of a convenience sample and quasi-experimental design may limit generalizability.

title: Secretory expression of tetrameric neuraminidase enhanced by signal peptide optimization elicits robust immunity against influenza infection in mice
abstract: Neuraminidase (NA), a key surface glycoprotein of influenza viruses, represents a more conserved antigenic target than hemagglutinin (HA) and has attracted interest as a potential target for vaccines with broader protective capacity. Nevertheless, the inefficient secretory production of tetrameric NA that maintain tetramer-like structural features remains challenging.Here, we developed an optimized signal peptide, opt-sp, by introducing valine and asparagine residues at the N-terminus of the Gaussia luciferase signal peptide (Gluc-sp) and incorporating a measles virus phosphoprotein-derived tetramerization domain. In a systematic comparison with three commonly used signal peptides, including tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), immunoglobulin G signal peptide (IgG-sp), and Gluc-sp, opt-sp was associated with increased relative secretion of NA protein under the tested expression conditions. Native PAGE analysis further suggested the presence of tetramer-like NA species. In mice,a DNA vaccine encoding opt-sp-fused NA elicited substantially stronger NA-specific humoral and cellular immune responses than constructs bearing conventional signal peptides and provided improved protection against homologous A/California/04/2009 (H1N1) challenge. These findings identify opt-sp as a promising signal peptide candidate for improving recombinant NA secretion and support further evaluation of this strategy for NA-based influenza vaccine development, including future studies of heterologous protection.

title_zh: 通过信号肽优化增强四聚体神经氨酸酶的分泌表达,在小鼠中引发针对流感感染的强大免疫力
source_body_en: Neuraminidase (NA), a key surface glycoprotein of influenza viruses, represents a more conserved antigenic target than hemagglutinin (HA) and has attracted interest as a potential target for vaccines with broader protective capacity. Nevertheless, the inefficient secretory production of tetrameric NA that maintain tetramer-like structural features remains challenging.Here, we developed an optimized signal peptide, opt-sp, by introducing valine and asparagine residues at the N-terminus of the Gaussia luciferase signal peptide (Gluc-sp) and incorporating a measles virus phosphoprotein-derived tetramerization domain. In a systematic comparison with three commonly used signal peptides, including tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), immunoglobulin G signal peptide (IgG-sp), and Gluc-sp, opt-sp was associated with increased relative secretion of NA protein under the tested expression conditions. Native PAGE analysis further suggested the presence of tetramer-like NA species. In mice,a DNA vaccine encoding opt-sp-fused NA elicited substantially stronger NA-specific humoral and cellular immune responses than constructs bearing conventional signal peptides and provided improved protection against homologous A/California/04/2009 (H1N1) challenge. These findings identify opt-sp as a promising signal peptide candidate for improving recombinant NA secretion and support further evaluation of this strategy for NA-based influenza vaccine development, including future studies of heterologous protection.
abstract_zh: 神经氨酸酶 (NA) 是流感病毒的一种关键表面糖蛋白,代表比血凝素 (HA) 更保守的抗原靶点,作为具有更广泛保护能力的 疫苗 的潜在靶点引起了人们的兴趣。然而,保持四聚体样结构特征的四聚体NA的低效分泌生产仍然具有挑战性。在这里,我们通过在高斯荧光素酶信号肽(Gluc-sp)的N末端引入缬氨酸和天冬酰胺残基并整合麻疹病毒磷蛋白衍生的四聚化结构域,开发了一种优化的信号肽opt-sp。在与三种常用信号肽(包括组织纤溶酶原激活剂 (tPA)、免疫球蛋白 G 信号肽 (IgG-sp) 和 Gluc-sp)的系统比较中,opt-sp 在测试的表达条件下与 NA 蛋白的相对分泌增加相关。天然 PAGE 分析进一步表明存在四聚体样 NA 物种。在小鼠中,编码 opt-sp 融合 NA 的 DNA 疫苗 比带有传统信号肽的构建体引发了更强的 NA 特异性体液和细胞 免疫应答,并提供了针对同源 A/California/04/2009 (H1N1) 攻击的改进保护。这些发现将 opt-sp 确定为改善重组 NA 分泌的有前途的信号肽候选者,并支持进一步评估这种基于 NA 的流感 疫苗 开发策略,包括异源保护的未来研究。

elements_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved in vitro experiments using influenza A viral cores, conducted in a laboratory setting with specific pH conditions applied to visualize structural changes.
elements_en.methods: The researchers used gel electrophoresis and protein staining to analyze the disassembly of the viral core under varying acidic conditions, as demonstrated in the video.
elements_en.main_results: Gel electrophoresis and protein staining revealed the progressive disassembly of the core structure under acidic conditions, indicating a pH-dependent solubilization process.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as evidence of pH-induced structural changes in the viral core, offering a novel visualization method for studying influenza A virus disassembly.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings contribute to understanding the environmental factors that affect influenza A virus stability, which could inform future research on viral behavior and potential therapeutic targets.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro conditions and does not account for in vivo factors, but the evidence is strong based on direct visualization techniques and clear experimental results.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及在实验室特定pH条件下进行的流感A病毒核心体外实验,以可视化结构变化。

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a tool for tracking viral infections, addressing the need for better understanding of influenza dynamics and intervention effects.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study describes a method for tracking viral infections in mouse models using a recombinant influenza A virus that expresses luciferase and fluorescence proteins.
analysis.methods: The method involves creating a recombinant influenza A virus that expresses both luciferase and fluorescence proteins, allowing for live imaging and quantification of viral infection in mouse models.
analysis.main_results: The method enables both in vivo and ex vivo studies, providing researchers with insights into viral dynamics and the effects of interventions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret this method as a novel approach that enhances the ability to study viral infections and their responses to interventions in real-time.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This method can inform future studies on viral dynamics and intervention efficacy, contributing to improved surveillance and understanding of influenza transmission.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to mouse models, which may not fully represent human influenza dynamics, and the evidence is based on a single method described in the abstract, resulting in moderate confidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a luciferase-fluorescent reporter influenza virus designed to track viral infections in mouse models. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在开发一种追踪病毒感染的工具,以应对更好地理解流感动态及其干预效果的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究描述了一种利用重组流感A病毒(该病毒表达荧光素酶和荧光蛋白)在小鼠模型中追踪病毒感染的方法。
elements_zh.methods: 该方法涉及构建一种重组流感A病毒,使其同时表达荧光素酶和荧光蛋白,从而允许在小鼠模型中进行病毒感染的活体成像和量化分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 该方法使研究人员能够进行体内和体外研究,从而获得关于病毒动态及其干预效果的见解。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将此方法解释为一种新颖的手段,能够增强对病毒感染及其对干预措施反应的实时研究能力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该方法可以为未来关于病毒动态和干预效果的研究提供信息,有助于改善监测和对流感传播的理解。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于小鼠模型,这可能无法完全代表人类流感的动态,且证据基于摘要中描述的单一方法,因此信心度中等。
